children: By Mark R. Long

Progress toward a U.S.-Mexico tariff deal has stalled amid opposition from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, according to people familiar with the talks. The Wall Street Journal's Gavin Bade and Santiago Pérez write that the U.S. and Mexico had been zeroing in on a deal that would reduce U.S. levies on steel, aluminum and automobiles in exchange for a series of concessions from Mexico.

A deal would pave the way for further talks on renewing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. In recent days, however, progress slowed considerably because of disagreements over the U.S. levies on vehicles and metals, which are imposed on national-security grounds and administered by Lutnick's department. Officials on both sides said the talks continue and denied there was any impasse.

Lutnick has opposed significant reductions in the 25% tariff on Mexican automobiles and the 50% levies on steel and aluminum, the people said. He also objected to reductions in tariffs on so-called derivative products-finished products made of steel and aluminum. Domestic aluminum companies have told the administration that any reduction in these levies would undermine U.S.-based firms.
China's Ministry of Commerce proposed new export controls on 40 technologies in the AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics sectors. (WSJ)
Quotable
"Rebalancing is less about selling more to China. It's about having China sell less to us."Tomas Baert, a trade adviser to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen
Trucking
J.B. Hunt Transport Services is looking to raise prices as it grapples with a steep increase in costs, the Journal's Elias Schisgall writes.

The logistics company has encountered a confluence of higher fuel costs, insurance claims and medical costs, as well as investments in new drivers to meet demand, which together hit operating income by more than $50 million from the second quarter to the third quarter.

As a result, J.B. Hunt is turning to price increases to recoup costs, executives said on a call after the Lowell, Ark., company posted higher year-over-year profit in the third quarter, despite the higher expenses. Some of these costs are expected to persist in the current quarter and into next year.

The quarter's intermodal revenue grew 20%, to $1.83 billion, with volume up 8%. Truckload revenue rose 37% and dedicated contract services revenue grew 11%. Revenue from final-mile services, however, slid 3%, to $200 million.
U.S. for-hire trucking employment rose in September from a year earlier for the first time in 41 months, climbing to 1.45 million workers, according to the Labor Department. (Journal of Commerce)
The head of the Alabama Trucking Association, Mark Colson, was named as the next CEO of the American Trucking Associations. (TruckingDive)
Number of the Day

Year-over-year increase in the producer-price index for the transportation and warehousing industries in September, while the overall U.S. PPI rose 6.3% from a year earlier, according to the Labor Department
Energy & Data Centers
Venture Global is aiming to build gas-fired generation to supply electricity to AI data centers, the WSJ's Jennifer Hiller and Benoît Morenne write.

The natural-gas exporter said it entered into agreements with GE Vernova and Baker Hughes Energy Services to procure equipment for on-site power plants, including turbines and transformers, which have been in high demand. The deals will allow Venture Global over time to make up to 10 gigawatts of computing capacity available at sites the company owns or controls.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. raised the prospect of adding to its U.S. manufacturing capacity beyond Arizona, potentially in Texas. (WSJ)
Meta Platforms and the government of Mason County, Ky., reached an agreement for the development of a data-center campus southeast of Cincinnati. (Lexington Herald-Leader)
In Other News
Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries, accusing Moscow of violating President Trump's ceasefire on energy targets. (WSJ)
U.S. retail sales rose by 0.8% in September to $745 billion, slowing from a 1.3% increase in August, according to the Commerce Department. (WSJ)
The eurozone goods trade swung to a deficit of the equivalent of $18.07 billion in August from a surplus of about $12.06 billion euros in July. (WSJ)
Canadian factory shipments increased 1.5% in August from the previous month. (WSJ)
Eurozone industrial output fell 0.5% in August, the third consecutive monthly decline. (WSJ)
Penske Automotive Group has agreed to be taken private by its biggest investors-Penske and Mitsui-in a deal giving the company an enterprise value of about $16.3 billion. (WSJ)
Lyft is establishing a new chauffeuring brand, called Alcove, that caters to demand for full days of executive travel between client meetings, conferences and flights. (WSJ)
Antofagasta lowered its copper-output forecast for next year. (WSJ)
Cosco Shipping's car-carrier unit signed a 10-year deal with Chinese automaker DFSK to expand shipping volumes and develop a global route network. (Splash247)
Merck plans to invest $2.9 billion to expand research and manufacturing of vaccines and other medicines in Pennsylvania by the end of 2030. (SupplyChain24/7)
A.P. Moller Capital said in a news release that it agreed to acquire Singapore-based ports operator Portek from Mitsui. Terms of the deal weren't disclosed.
South Korean carrier HMM plans to invest $1.62 billion to expand its containership fleet. (TradeWinds)
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approved a $2.3 billion project to build a new container terminal at the Port of Savannah. (SupplyChainBrain)
